snippet.textDisplay:
By 2026, several major milestones Elon Musk confidently guaranteed would happen by now have completely failed to materialize:

1. Unsupervised Full Self-Driving & 1 Million Robotaxis (Target: 2020)
• The Prediction: In 2019, Musk famously declared that Tesla would have 1 million fully autonomous robotaxis on the road by 2020. He later predicted in July 2025 that autonomous ride-hailing would cover half the U.S. population by the end of that year.

• The Reality: Tesla vehicles still operate under "supervised" Full Self-Driving (FSD), requiring active human attention. The actual driverless robotaxi fleet consists of small, localized pilots (such as roughly 30 monitored vehicles in Austin) rather than a mass-market commercial reality.

2. A Manned Mission to Mars (Target: 2025)
• The Prediction: For over a decade, Musk target-dated human arrival on Mars. He frequently pointed to 2024 or 2025 as the deadline for SpaceX's first crewed mission to the Red Planet.

• The Reality: While SpaceX's Starship development continues, the vehicle has yet to ferry astronauts to the Moon—let alone Mars. NASA and industry scientists maintain that human footprints on Mars are highly unlikely until the mid-2030s.

3. Mass Scaling of the Optimus Humanoid Robot (Target: 2025)
• The Prediction: Musk originally forecast that Tesla would produce 5,000 Optimus humanoid robots in 2025, paving the way for 50,000 units by 2026.
• The Reality: Due to engineering bottlenecks—particularly with perfecting the robot's hands—Tesla completely abandoned its 2025 target. Factory mass production is not expected to even begin until the tail end of 2026.

4. A Hovering Tesla Roadster & Flying Car Demo (Target: 2025)
• The Prediction: In late 2025, Musk guaranteed that Tesla would unveil a spectacular product demonstration for the next-generation Tesla Roadster before the end of the year, hinting it might feature SpaceX thrusters that would allow it to hover.
• The Reality: 2025 closed with no Roadster demonstration, no flying car prototype, and no production timeline in sight.

5. Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) (Target: 2025)
• The Prediction: Musk predicted that his AI startup, xAI, would successfully develop Artificial General Intelligence (AGI)—an AI that surpasses human capability at almost all tasks—by 2025.
• The Reality: xAI missed this window, prompting Musk to quietly adjust his expectations and officially push his prediction for the emergence of AGI out to 2026.

He who pays, decides.

If you think that in the future everything will be free, you still do not understand human nature. Nothing is truly free when someone else pays the bill.

The moment money loses its meaning and robots take over most of human labor, a more fundamental question arises: 
on what, then, will the independence of the citizen still rest?

Whoever becomes entirely dependent for his livelihood on a state that provides for his basic needs, runs the risk that dependence will gradually turn into obedience. For whoever controls the means on which others depend, thereby also gains influence over their choices.

And whoever believes that this power will remain limited to money and provisions, and that the state will never interfere with the upbringing of children, the organization of family life, or the way citizens are expected to behave, underestimates the nature of power. Power has a tendency to expand when it is not restrained by freedom, responsibility, and limits.

The deepest question, therefore, is not whether robots will take over our jobs or whether money will ever disappear. The real question is:

Who will determine the conditions under which man is permitted to live?

For as soon as someone structurally determines that on which you depend, that someone will ultimately also determine a part of your freedom.

He who pays, decides — and he who is entirely dependent may in the end pay with the most precious thing he possesses: his independence.

snippet.textDisplay:
AI, Metaphysics, and the Unseen: The Blind Leading the Blind

We are living in an age where machines now “think” in ways that leave even their creators uneasy while AI shocks investors and engineers.

Ego enters before understanding begins.

Meanwhile, the real questions are almost ignored.
•	What is mind?
•	What is consciousness?
•	What is the unseen aspect of reality?
•	What does it mean that our tiny planet is like a grain of sand in a cosmic desert?
•	What happens when our technology races ahead of our metaphysical and moral maturity?

Modern AI sits uncomfortably in this landscape.

We have built systems that mimic aspects of human perception, memory and language. We do not, however, have a serious answer to what consciousness actually is. We do not know what “self” really means. We barely understand our own sensory and cognitive apparatus, yet we are confident enough to declare metaphysics “irrational” and the unseen “nonexistent”.

That confidence is not science. It is arrogance.
The irony is brutal:
•	Many of the people most excited about AI have deep technical skill but almost no training in theology, metaphysics, or ethics.
•	Many of the people with spiritual sensitivity and scriptural depth have no institutional platform in the AI conversation.

So the world is now watching the blind lead the blind — both morally and metaphysically — with increasingly powerful tools in their hands.

AI is not just a gadget. It is a test.

It is testing whether we will finally admit the limits of materialism.  

It is testing whether religious communities can move beyond tribal defensiveness to serious reflection on the nature of reality.  

It is testing whether scholars, technologists, and believers can sit at the same table and ask: “What kind of world are we building, and according to which understanding of existence?”

snippet.textDisplay:
The Grand Designer and the Illusion of Human Control

Humanity stands today at a remarkable threshold.

We have built machines that can process information at extraordinary speed, generate language, recognize patterns, create images, reason through complex problems, and perform tasks that once seemed uniquely human. We call this achievement artificial intelligence.

And yet, in the midst of our amazement, perhaps we have forgotten something fundamental.

Who gave humanity the intelligence with which it built intelligence?

The believer’s answer is simple: God.

God is omnipotent.
God is omniscient.
God is omnipresent.
God is omnibenevolent.

If God is the Creator of all that exists, then nothing created by humanity exists outside His knowledge, His awareness, or His ultimate sovereignty.

Humanity did not create intelligence itself. Humanity discovered, developed, organized, and applied abilities that were already part of the created order.

We did not create the laws of mathematics.
We did not create consciousness.
We did not create matter.
We did not create time and space.
We did not create the universe.
We did not place the stars in their galaxies.
We did not create the invisible foundations upon which the visible world depends.

And yet, having achieved remarkable technological progress, humanity can sometimes behave as though it has become the master of creation.

That is where humility becomes necessary.

Look at our position in the cosmos.

The Earth, immense to us, is unimaginably small compared with the universe. Humanity occupies an almost incomprehensibly tiny place within a creation whose scale we can scarcely perceive.

And still, we argue, compete, accumulate, dominate, destroy, and congratulate ourselves on our intelligence.

We have built artificial intelligence—and now we are afraid of it.

We wonder whether the intelligence we created might one day surpass us, overpower us, replace us, or escape our control.

But perhaps the deeper question is not:

“Will AI control humanity?”

Perhaps the deeper question is:

“Why does humanity believe that it is ultimately in control of anything?”

If one believes in God as the Creator of everything, then AI is not an independent force that has suddenly appeared outside the Creator’s awareness.

It is part of a world whose possibilities were already known to God.

Humanity may perceive AI as a sudden technological revolution. God, in the believer’s understanding, is not surprised by it.

Humanity sees a few decades of technological development.

God sees the entirety of history.

Humanity sees algorithms, processors, data centers, machines and mathematical models.

God sees the whole of creation.

Humanity sees its own intelligence as extraordinary.

God is the source of the very capacity by which humanity is able to think.

So perhaps the extraordinary rise of AI should not merely produce fear.

Perhaps it should produce humility.

AI may become extraordinarily capable. It may transform economies, education, science, medicine, communication, creativity, warfare, work, and countless other aspects of human life. It may force humanity to confront questions about intelligence, consciousness, identity, purpose, and the meaning of being human.

But whatever happens, humanity should not confuse technological power with ultimate power.

A creature remains a creature, however sophisticated its creations become.

A human being may construct a machine capable of processing billions of calculations, but that does not make humanity the author of existence itself.

We should therefore be careful about the arrogance hidden inside the phrase:

“We created AI.”

Yes, humanity developed AI.

But humanity did so within a universe it did not create, using laws it did not invent, matter it did not manufacture, mathematics it did not author, and intelligence whose ultimate origin remains a profound question.

The machine may become more powerful.

Human knowledge may expand.

Technology may reach levels that today’s generation can barely imagine.

The boundaries between biology, computation, physical reality, and virtual reality may continue to evolve.

And perhaps these developments will take humanity into intellectual and spiritual territory it has never previously encountered.

But none of this necessarily means that humanity has escaped the limits of creation.

Perhaps it means the opposite.

Perhaps the astonishing progression of AI is another reminder of how little humanity truly understands about the reality in which it exists.

The great danger may therefore not be AI itself.

The greater danger may be humanity’s illusion of self-sufficiency.

We fear that our creation might one day become our master, while forgetting that we ourselves are not masters of creation.

We worry about losing control over machines while overlooking how little control we possess over the universe, time, mortality, nature, and ultimately our own existence.

This is the moment for humility.

Not humiliation.

Not despair.

Humility.

To recognize that intelligence is not the same as omniscience.

Power is not the same as omnipotence.

Presence is not omnipresence.

Prediction is not divine knowledge.

And technological creation is not creation from nothing.

Humanity may continue to climb the mountain of knowledge.

AI may become one of the greatest instruments humanity has ever developed.

The journey ahead may be astonishing.

But humanity should never mistake the instrument for the Author, the creation for the Creator, or the discovery of another layer of reality for mastery over reality itself.

For the believer, the ultimate perspective is unchanged:

God remains God.

Humanity remains humanity.

AI remains something created within the order of creation.

And whatever unimaginable future lies ahead—whether material, intellectual, technological, or spiritual—it unfolds under a reality infinitely greater than the human mind can comprehend.

Perhaps the greatest lesson of the AI age will therefore not be how intelligent machines can become.

Perhaps it will be how little humanity has understood about the true scale of intelligence, creation, existence, and God.

We stand at the edge of something extraordinary.

Let us explore it.

Let us learn from it.

Let us use it responsibly.

But above all, let us remember our place.

We are not the Grand Designers.

We are creatures living within a creation vastly greater than ourselves.

And if God is truly the Creator of all things, then the future does not belong ultimately to humanity, nor to its machines.

Ultimately, it belongs to God.

Digital intelligence can never exceed human intelligence.

One needs to understand biological systems thoroughly enough to be able to understand, what biology is able to do, while technical devices, no matter how sophisticatedly they might be programmed today, may it be an autopilot, that takes a Boeing 747 from Frankfurt to Buenos Aires in 14 hours and lands it there or what have you ....

A pocket calculator will  n e v e r  develop anything near what is called "intuition", a piece of metal or semi-conductor, materia has its own laws and functions, but the can never reach the capacity of biological tissues, organs and organisms, which have millions of years of development and experience passed on in the genes.

No way such thing is thinkable.

A living cell is something far different than a technical device, a programmed robot etc.

It was clearly fascinating, 40 years back in school, when we purchased our first order for 25 calculators from Germany to Texas Instruments in 1977 and after everyone had his own pocket-calculator, to see, how fast that thing would calculate anything you press into the buttons, much faster, than any person could do.

The calculstor was faster, yes, but it could do only, what you told it to do.

That principle hasn't changed and will never change.

The machine will never be able to "be the master" over man.

The machine can perform certain things faster and more precise, but it doesn't "think". It performs orders without thinking.

Some of the computers executions might seem to be "intelligent", but they aren't actually intelligence, because they perform, what they were programmed to do.

The term artificial "intelligence" is also not appropriate, because intelligence includes the possibility to create something completely new by own contemplation, which the machine, the calculator, the computer cannot perform.

It cannot bring out more, than what it was programmed to do.

That's why the term "intelligence" is not actually appropriate to apply it in terms of a device, a computer etc. .

Intelligence in the biological sense also includes emotions, and a piece of metal doesn't "feel" cold or heat.

It is therefore not appropriate to postulate, that at any time now or in the future any material device will surpass the human being in terms of intelligence.

My biro, my calculator, my sunglasses are very welcome items, but non of those or whaterver technical device -
may it be able to calculate "faster than" myself - it will never be able to come anywhere close to what human intelligence actually is, 
because the device will never 
really  b e  intelligent in the biological sense.

It cannot - due to the lack of consciousness.

One might programme a robot
to talk about God 
by programming 
all of Immanuel Kants books
into the computer, 
the robot has no conscience 
to understand, what God is.

It can only eject the words programmed into it, but there will never  b e 
conscious understanding 
by the device.

That is clear.

An therefore it is impropper to talk of "intelligence" concerning a robot or computer.

It is a little bit funny and also questionable, why science has decided to call the capacity to calculate and compute "intelligence".

It seems, that there needs to be 
a sober definition 
of the term "intelligence" 
according to the ancient Greek philosophical platonic tradition
of defining terms.

This might bring along 
the ability to differenciate between 
- human, intellectual, rational, emotional, experience-based intelligence    and
- robotric programmed calculator- and data-based combinatory capacity.

Yet, in no way 
will a robot 
come anywhere near human intelligence, this can already be said in advance.

snippet.textDisplay:
This company doesn’t show a single video that demonstrates real value as an industrial robot. It’s always just acrobatics, and China has already dominated that space. They never present any footage proving actual industrial usefulness—just this kind of thing over and over—probably because someone there thinks it looks cool and impressive.

In the past, when they tried to show a real industrial scenario, Atlas wearing a hot dog costume couldn’t do anything and just failed. And now, calling this version “mass-producible” is almost comical. Does that mean the previous version was only made just for show? No other robotics company makes that kind of distinction. It all just feels like more performance for display.

Right now, humanoid robots still struggle with even simple tasks like folding clothes or moving objects, because they have to deal with detailed, unpredictable real-world variables. Meanwhile, these perfectly staged, pre-programmed acrobatic routines have already become the easier part. And even then, they don’t seem confident—these clips are only a few dozen seconds long at most.

How long are they going to keep putting on this kind of show?

snippet.textDisplay:
The fact that people still laugh at the idea of robots replacing humans is honestly wild. We’re already living through it. Companies like Amazon use massive robotic systems in warehouses, reducing the need for human labor in many areas, while factories owned by Tesla and Foxconn heavily rely on automation to cut costs and increase efficiency. AI is now replacing not only factory work, but also customer support, art, coding, and even office jobs.

People act like it’s some sci-fi fantasy, but the reality is already here. A robot doesn’t get tired, ask for salary raises, or need sleep. Denying that machines can outperform the average human in specific tasks at this point is just coping with reality.

snippet.textDisplay:
​@kebabfotoWARNING: This will be long, so if you don't want to read it, don't. No need to be insufferable and tell me you're not reading it. 

I'm speaking about your claim that robots couldn't replace us anytime soon. Again, if you actually believe that, you haven't been paying attention to the past 25 years. 

I'm a CPU architect, bro. I'm around this stuff every single day. If you have a pc and use AMD, then you almost certainly use a CPU I helped to design. MSDMT Dual Degree (Master of Science: Digital and Material Technologies), and I also specialize in large language models, neural networking, and digital to biological data transference (DNA data transference). I'm not someone who will speak about something I'm unsure of, unlike the other 99.99% of the population of grown children who will refuse correction for the sake of their own pride, regardless of whether they know they're wrong or not. 

Computer performance doubles about every 18 months to 2 years. Thanks to neural networking and A.I., robotics performance doubles about every 7 to 9 months. They can already perform most tasks on a scale physically impossible for a human to reach. Look at the robot on in the video. Did it trip? Yes, but it was also handicapped by designing it to be much more inefficient simply because we want them to look like us. What most people seem to be missing is that despite these shortcomings, despite tripping, this robot can already dance better than 99% of the population. You would marvel at some of the things I've seen in the industry. I'll put it to you as simply as I can- what does your common sense tell you, now that you're seeing this- that robotics are much worse behind the scenes, or significantly better? 

I always use this as an example as to how far we've come, because any gamers or pc enthusiasts can typically relate to it- storage (which is essential to robotics as well), is pretty easy to come by. Today, you can buy 1tb of high-speed solid-state storage for about $80, and it would be the size and thickness of a stick of chewing gum. In the year 2000, that same 1tb of solid-state would have ran about 10 million dollars, and would have been the size of a refrigerator. Robotics are advancing at more than double that rate. If that doesn't put things into perspective for you, nothing will.

snippet.textDisplay: The problem is that the design team tried to have all three sides of this imaginary triangle be true at once, but you can really only have two sides at a time. 1) They wanted Starscream to true 1:1 to an F-22, 2) they wanted Starscream to be less than or equal to Megatron's height, and 3) they wanted Megatron to just be a *little* bigger than Optimus so they could realistically exchange blows. But it doesn't work that way. That forest fight was a huge cheat. Since Megs, Optimus and Grindor all scaled pretty realistically, I think they just shrunk Starscream to make it feel even.

snippet.textDisplay: It makes sense for Starscream to be compressed compared to his jet form. A jet doesn't have as much mass per cubic meter as, say, a tank, which needs more armor and a more versatile structure to handle a wider variety of loads. A giant robot that exchanges  frequent, random, and often violent forces with the environment would need to consolidate the specialized, weight-saving members that make for a viable aircraft into structures with more redundancy. Regardless of how strong Cybertronian materials are, a humanoid can afford to be denser than an aircraft, and it should be if it's going to get punched and shot at all of the time.

snippet.textDisplay:
Ehh this video doesn’t really have the full picture in mind. At 31 feet tall and ~30 feet wide at the shoulders, Bayverse Starscream is a pretty chunky and huge robot, but he’s still outclassed in all measurable dimensions by his 62 foot long and 44 foot wide F-22 alt. Even the more hollow and thin sections of the jet can’t really account for the sheer amount of stretching Screamer has to do given how gappy and hollow his robot mode is (you can see through pretty much all of his limbs and body due to the thin framework under the larger armor chunks). Of course, he’s not mass shifting by an insane degree either. Just enough so that you don’t really notice, which was the intent behind the scale of the Bayverse. No obvious mass shifting like gun Megatron, but still some reasonable areas of shapeshifting sci-fi nonsense

In BB, however, the rule does indeed change complete. The Seekers are only 18 feet tall in that film. Blitzwing turns into a 63 foot long F-4 Phantom II. Pretty much everyone mass shifts in the new films, but it’s especially bad with the Seekers. That’s not really a problem, sci-fi technology and all, but it is whacky to imagine

snippet.textDisplay:
Im curious if ill get pushback on this but i actually preferred early bayverse designs to g1. The robotic skeleton look was so clever. And the way they transformed were so much more satisfying to watch than g1. Especially since (for the most part) they took details like this in and kept sizing more or less accurate. It felt more realistic for them to be able to transform. And they looked like what they were. Giant alien robots. 

One comon criticism i hear as well is that all the decepticons were dull colors which made things uninteresting. But in a sense that was the point. They were military vehicles that were trying to blend in. If they had red and blue streaked across them theyd stand out. Besides. Its not like they didnt use color when not appreciate. Look at barricade. 

Even in bumblebee. I liked the fusion of the two designs and transformation styles. But i personally find it less interesting in terms of color because now you lose the ability to make them military vehicles which i thought was such a clever idea. Decepticons are a military group so it makes sense thematically. But also they are tryna infiltrate the millitary so it works for the plot too.

snippet.textDisplay:
I don't mind the design of Starscream in the Bay films.

But please, let's not forget that these are Cybertronians. Starscream is not made out of a jet. He transforms into one. The whole point of their body is that they can morph themselves to fit a form.

So it is plausible that Starscream could morph his body into something the size of one of those jets. He would be at least three times heavier than one of those things considering how dense Cybertronians are. Which means he has a lot more mass tucked into a smaller space that he can expand outward into larger shapes.

We don't have to make arguments for realism. These are transformers. I liked the design, but let's not try to justify it with physics when we have magical robots that can transform into anything and that live for millions of years.

This is just nerdy, revisionist history at work. There was no deep "logic" in how Movie Starscream looked. When the first movie hit, they were determined to make their robot designs stand out from what we normally expected to see. Partly because the concept artists were heavily skeptical of how good G1 designs would work on film but, also because they wanted to differentiate the film to be "their own".

Which it succeeded in doing. Movie bots look NOTHING like Transformers in other series and universes.

snippet.textDisplay: @1107Archangel Yeah but there is a way you can explain that the aliens look like us because the quintessons (whoever the squid guys are) once saw humans and modelled the robots after them and that is why Cybertronian look like us.  I looked at some of the more good designs of the Bayverse like Nemesis Prime and realised if all the Bayformers looked as cool as that, then the G1 fans wouldn't have bashed the bayverse so much.  My fave Live Action Optimus Prime is still the one from Transformers Bumblebee. And that's not just nostalgia, I just like the "solid" look more. Having little gaps all over the place makes them look vulnerable. Like if you were to remove the frame of your car so that the engine is always exposed, it just looks worse and also you lose the aerodynamic benefits of the frame pushing air away from the car as it moves at high speed.  The robots should also feel "covered" if you know what I mean...It's just a preference. The word I will use is "over-engineered". IE that they chose to fold panels up and make a lot of unecessary steps to get to the final form but the final form is super messy and one of the biggest criticism of the design everytime you see a fight scene. You can barely tell what part of the guys body hit what part of the opponents body since our eyes can barely make out what they are doing. Why sci-fi or fantasy movies still have to be somewhat grounded in real-world physics (i.e our understanding/perception of the world), bcs it's what keeps whatever conflict and stakes in the movie still matter in audience's mind. 

If writers decide to go carte blanche with the whole "sci-fi fantasy characters can do whatever they want", then what stops the writer from having deus ex machina and keep slipping in new powers/abilities whenever it's convenient?

snippet.textDisplay:
People say we shouldn’t be afraid or ashamed of making mistakes. And honestly, it’s true… because the more we feed the idea that mistakes are something embarrassing, the more we move away from learning, growing, and truly living. Human beings are fragile — that’s reality. But we are also capable of getting back up again and again. And sometimes companionship, support, and understanding can carry the soul all the way into the stratosphere.
Everything moves so fast. Life moves fast. Learning takes time too. So how many times do you think Michael Jackson ❤made mistakes practicing those dance moves? Do you think he felt ashamed repeating them over and over again? To become who he became, he probably had to fail, adjust, repeat, and try again countless times.
So bravo to the people who make mistakes and keep going. Because continuing forward, even with fear, is also a form of courage.

snippet.textDisplay:
For many reasons, this is one of the funniest videos of robots attempting human tasks on the entire internet. Utterly hilarious watching the robot being dragged off the stage as a ruined collection of machine parts, by its shirt. What on Earth were they thinking? Getting a little ahead of ourselves, aren't we, there? 
I think it's the part where  the robot attempts to scramble up two steps, and the complete chaos that ensues, that makes me laugh. No matter how many times I watch it (and I'm probably now close to 100), I burst out laughing from the moment the robot bumps into the first step, and attempts to recover.  
Watching it scramble, and finally collapse, sends me over the top every single time. I'm sure the parts can be useful for something - a sewing machine, a toaster, or a slightly used and  dented companion for some spinster - as long as it just has to sit quietly.

​@moldycat4852it's a private company & the vast majority of people including those disabled are more interested in robots than clunky exosuits? With robots we can obtain a post scarcity society, which is far more important than letting a few more disabled people shuffle around, let alone when we're closer to treating & curing these conditions than making a comfortable anthro-mobility device.

We should focus on treating & curing people, not strapping them to ungainly machines... wearing knee & elbow braces sucks enough, let alone a cast & let alone something connected to motors & chunky frames. Enjoyable anthro-mobility devices literally aren't going to exist without intense micro-fluidics & soft robotics, squeezed into something that fits like a sock or t shirt, anything else will always suck.

If people making robots (even disgusting looking ones like these) bothers you so much, just design a mobility aid? We live in a free market, so there's literally nothing stopping you? If it's good, people will buy it? That's just how things work? I think mindless capitalism sucks, but there's a good chance things would be a lot worse for disabled people if there wasn't some degree of competition in providing them said devices & medicine? So just claiming that everyones money should be spent on flawed devices, just because, is inane.

snippet.textDisplay: There’s something a little backwards about celebrating robots that run half marathons. Are those the breakthroughs that matter? Endurance running is a flashy demo, but it’s not where real-world value lives. Nobody’s lining up to buy a robot because it can jog 13 miles without collapsing. What actually matters is fine motor control, precision, and reliability under delicate conditions. Can it assemble sensitive electronics without damaging them? Can it handle variability and still perform exact tasks like threading a needle or assembling microscopic components? That’s the difference between a novelty and a tool that reshapes industries. Right now, these demonstrations are more like marketing theater than meaningful progress.

snippet.textDisplay:
This is gonna sound angrier than I am about it, I'm mostly just confused. Comparing it to the men's world record would be like entering an RC car into the Boston marathon. Like yeah... We know the robots can run better. 

Honestly the biggest limitation you're imposing on yourself is the humanoid body plan. These robots would be faster on just wheels, or as quadrupeds, so limiting yourself to "looks like people" is really the biggest challenge, and you still have to make tradeoffs in the body plan to make it a fast runner that would make it bad at other stuff, so I'm not really understanding the point here. If we wanna optimize for speed then why impose the limitation of running on 2 legs? Humans run on 2 legs to be able to throw things while running, these robots can't, and don't need to do that, so let them run like a cheetah and go fast, or a car and go super fast. 

If you want a fast robot, make a fast robot. If you want a robot that looks like a person, make a robot that looks like a person. Wanting a robot that's just good at running marathons feels like we're looking for excuses to throw robots at imaginary problems. Battle bots don't stand on 2 feet like boxers do, so why do these robots gotta look like people to race? 

I get that this is a competition and the fact that the end designs of the robots are useless for anything but winning this competition is just how it goes. Like F1 has a lot of work that goes into it that has no advantages for anybody anywhere outside of F1 and that's totally fine, but nobody compares F1 to the 100 meter dash, so why are we comparing robot foot racing to human foot racing?

What actually happens:
Trade secrets theft – Employees or hackers steal proprietary data (manufacturing processes, formulas, source code).
Counterfeiting – Fake versions of branded goods (electronics, clothing, pharmaceuticals).
Patent/IP infringement – Companies replicate designs or tech without licensing.
Cyber espionage – State-linked groups targeting foreign firms or universities.
Why it’s associated with China:
Rapid industrial growth created incentives to “catch up” technologically.
Weak enforcement historically (though this has improved somewhat).
Some cases tied to state-backed actors or tolerated behavior at local levels.

@cassie6056  Take it from a Navy veteran and former Strike Warfare Officer: we have had fully autonomy weapon systems for literally decades now.

I know. Not only was I in charge of the ones onboard USS CARNEY (DDG-64), but I acted as BB ("Bravo Bravo"), the Joint Strike Force command radioman for CBG 6 (that was USS JOHN F KENNEDY at the time) coordinating the deployment of autonomous weapons and early-era drones in the lead up to the invasion of Iraq in 2001.

Not only has the technology come a long ways since then, now the weapon platforms themselves can use recognition systems for far more advanced target acquisition and friend-or-foe identification.

Note that we have been using fully autonomous weapons platforms since the 1980s. The AIM-54 Phoenix missile was completely fire-and-forget, utilizing information from the launch platform's radar systems and onboard FoF identification systems to track targets at long range and destroy them. All the weapons operator had to do was fire the missile; they didn't even need to designate a target.
